prompt: What question is a reviewer of an analyst's portfolio trying to answer, by the lesson?

choices.text: Whether the candidate knows the most popular dashboard tools
choices.why: A smaller question most candidates pass.

choices.text: Would this person turn our vague questions into decisions?
choices.why: Charts and tools answer only whether they can operate software.

choices.text: How many projects they have
choices.why: Evidence, not a museum.

choices.text: Whether they code
choices.why: Not the question named.

prompt: Which of these separate candidates, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Judgement about the question
choices.why: Starting from a decision.

choices.text: What they ruled out
choices.why: It shows how they think.

choices.text: Honesty about limits
choices.why: No limits reads as not yet found.

choices.text: The number of charts
choices.why: More charts is not better evidence.

prompt: Should Marina's failed first meeting appear in her case study?

choices.text: No, because a portfolio should show only successes to look professional
choices.why: The lesson calls the failure an asset.

choices.text: Only if the interviewer asks about failures directly during the conversation
choices.why: It belongs in the written story.

choices.text: No, because it would embarrass Paulo and Sandra, who were in that meeting
choices.why: Framed as what you changed, it embarrasses nobody.

choices.text: Yes: it shows you learn from a room
choices.why: "Here is what I changed" is one of the most persuasive sentences an analyst can write.

prompt: Put the first five parts of a case study in order.
Why does the one-page summary go on top of the case study?

choices.text: Because most reviewers will read only that page, so it has to stand alone
choices.why: The seven parts are for the interested, the files for the sceptic.

choices.text: For search engines
choices.why: No.

choices.text: Because it is the shortest
choices.why: Shortness is not the reason.

choices.text: Templates require it
choices.why: No.

prompt: How many parts, below the summary, does the lesson's case study have?
hint: From the question to what you learnt.

prompt: A case study runs to thirty pages. What problem does the lesson see?

choices.text: Reviewers will think the candidate has too much free time on their hands
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: It will not render well on a phone screen, where many reviewers read
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: It hands over the analysis, not its story
choices.why: Cut until every paragraph answers a question the reviewer would ask.

choices.text: It is too detailed
choices.why: Detail is not the issue; relevance is.

prompt: Which file in Faro's case study does a sceptical reviewer open second?

choices.text: The deck
choices.why: That shows the communication.

choices.text: The spreadsheet over the data
choices.why: Every number as a formula over the twenty-four rows.

choices.text: The decision log
choices.why: Useful, and not the second.

choices.text: The definitions
choices.why: Close, and not what the lesson names.

prompt: Your employer does not allow its data to be published. What is the first option the lesson suggests?

choices.text: Publish it anyway with the company name removed from every chart and table
choices.why: Removing a name is not permission.

choices.text: Describe it in the interview with the real numbers from memory instead
choices.why: That is the third option, without the numbers.

choices.text: Ask a colleague to publish it under their name so it is not traced to you
choices.why: That is still publishing what you may not.

choices.text: Recreate it on public data
choices.why: With the same shape, and saying you did.

prompt: Brazil's data protection law, which applies to anything that can identify a customer, is the ___.
Faro's cancellation result is still open. What does the lesson say to do with that in the case study?

choices.text: Say so: an open result stated plainly is part of an honest case study
choices.why: Saying it is part of the story.

choices.text: Leave it out
choices.why: Hiding it weakens trust.

choices.text: Estimate it
choices.why: Guessing a result is worse.

choices.text: Wait to publish
choices.why: The pilot result is already worth showing.

prompt: Which test asks whether somebody would act differently depending on the answer?

choices.text: Can you finish it in four to six weeks, given everything else you are doing?
choices.why: That is the size test.

choices.text: Can you show the data in public, or recreate it from a public source?
choices.why: That is the data test.

choices.text: Is there a decision?
choices.why: Real or plausible, someone who would act on it.

choices.text: Is it original?
choices.why: Not one of the three.

prompt: How does this lesson's case study relate to the portfolio-project course?

choices.text: They are two separate projects that should cover different questions
choices.why: That is building the same thing twice.

choices.text: One project: this is its analytical heart
choices.why: portfolio-project turns it into a finished public piece.

choices.text: The case study replaces the course
choices.why: Each adds what the other cannot.

choices.text: They are unrelated
choices.why: They share the project.

prompt: Match each portfolio-project lesson the case study feeds to what it adds.
At most how many weeks does the lesson's size test allow for the project?
Put the five-minute spoken version in order.
Why say the five minutes aloud at least three times before an interview?

choices.text: To memorise the slides in the right order so that none are skipped
choices.why: The point is not memory of slides.

choices.text: Because interviewers always ask for exactly five minutes and stop you at five
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: To sound less natural and more rehearsed, which interviewers prefer
choices.why: No.

choices.text: Sentences that read well run long when spoken
choices.why: And the sentence where you lose your thread is the one they remember.

prompt: After the five minutes, what does the lesson say to do?

choices.text: Stop and let them ask, because the questions teach them most about you
choices.why: Lesson 10's four moves work there too.

choices.text: Show the deck
choices.why: Only if asked.

choices.text: Summarise again
choices.why: Repetition wastes their time.

choices.text: Ask about salary
choices.why: Not here.

prompt: Which check from earlier lessons does the written version get before publishing?

choices.text: A spelling check of every title by a native speaker of the reviewer's language
choices.why: Useful, and not one of the two.

choices.text: A peer review by another analyst who has never seen the data before
choices.why: That is the red team, not one of the two named here.

choices.text: The headline test and the checklist
choices.why: Lesson 3's test and lesson 12's checklist.

choices.text: A legal review
choices.why: Not named.

prompt: A candidate's portfolio is a polished dashboard with no question, no decision and no limits. What does it show, by this lesson?

choices.text: That the candidate can turn vague questions into decisions
choices.why: Nothing in it shows that.

choices.text: That they can operate the software
choices.why: Which most candidates can; it misses the question the reviewer is asking.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: It shows a skill, just not the one that separates candidates.

choices.text: Strong judgement
choices.why: Judgement shows in the question and the decision.
